new_statements.quote: there exists clear evidence of a system of pitch accent or tone, with at least two degrees of prominence. [...] Smith River has pitch with these sharply limited distributions: a) All monosyllabic utterances, such as duu no and su? good, have high pitch. b) Every utterance has at least one high pitch. c) There are no polysyllabic utterances containing all high or all low pitches. d) Within a word, as tentatively identified, the maximum number of high pitches is two. [...] In summary, the Smith River suprasegmental system shows similarities to what has been called a pitch-accent system, in contrast with a pitch system like that of Navaho
new_statements.citation: Bright, Jane O. 1964. The Phonology of Smith River Athapaskan (Tolowa). International Journal of American Linguistics 30(2):101-107.
new_statements.locator: p. 104, section 3 (suprasegmentals); identity remark p. 101, section 0
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Re-opened (p.104 block, file lines ~260-303; two-column interleave) and cross-checked against a fresh extracted text of and the slice3 copy. All three quoted stretches are present word for word at sec. 3, p.104: 'there exists clear evidence of a system of pitch accent or tone, with at least two degrees of prominence'; 'Unlike the Apachean and Northern Athapaskan languages, Smith River has pitch with these sharply limited distributions: a) All monosyllabic utterances, such as duu no and su? good, have high pitch. b) Every utterance has at least one high pitch. c) There are no polysyllabic utterances containing all high or all low pitches. d) Within a word, as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tolowa(-Chetco) has a pitch accent system: prominence is realised as high pitch, every word/utterance carries at least one high-pitched syllable and a word carries at most two, but the source gives no rule locating the accented syllable by position, weight or morphology; accent position must be learned per word (contrasting pairs such as baasag 'bread' vs baaseh 'seagulls' are listed). Later work (Tuttle 1990 apud Doty & Guion 2007) reanalyses the same prominence as stress accent, again without a published placement rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Bright allows up to two high pitches within a word (constraint d) but does not rank them; Doty & Guion 2007 transcribe one 4-syllable word with primary on the penult and a secondary on the initial. No rule stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; Bright notes words are only 'tentatively identified'. Jacobs & Seaburg 1976 note that stress marks in the 1935 Chetco field transcription are unreliable (slash ambiguous between length and stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Bright's constraints a-c are phrased over utterances, d over the word; her contrasting pairs are citation forms. The description is of the Smith River (Tolowa, California) dialect; Chetco (Oregon) is named on p.101 as an almost mutually intelligible northern dialect and is not separately described. Community orthography (Bommelyn et al. 1972/1983, covering 'Smith River, Chetco, Tututni') marks the stressed syllable word by word with a diacritic, consistent with non-predictable placement.
new_statements.identity_note: chet1237 is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping code: Glottolog states Chetco and Tolowa 'are indistinguishable as languages' (citing Bommelyn 1997) and redirects to Tolowa-Chetco [tol] = tolo1259, which is ALREADY a catalog unit ( row tolo1259, coded from Bright 1964:104). The only first-hand prosodic statement is Bright 1964, which describes the Smith River (Tolowa proper, California) dialect and itself says Smith River is 'almost mutually intelligible with the more northern Athapaskan dialects spoken along the Winchuck and Chetco rivers' (p.101) -- i.e. it does not describe the Chetco dialect directly. For the Chetco dialect proper (Billy Metcalf, Siletz 1935), the only linguistic publications (Jacobs 1968; Jacobs & Seaburg 1976/1977) are texts whose introduction notes that stress was marked in the field transcription but gives no rule. Bommelyn et al.'s community textbook titles the language 'The Tolowa (Smith River, Chetco, Tututni) Language'. Adding chet1237 as its own catalog entry would double-count tolo1259 (a retired code does not make a separate language).

new_statements.quote: A. Proposed Rules for Accentuation: 1. The domain of stress is bounded by the right edge of the stem. 2. Stress the last vowel in the domain. 3. Stress all full vowels. 4. The strongest stress in a word is the rightmost stress. B. Phonetic Realization. An accented vowel is realized with high pitch. Generally, if there are two accented vowels in adjacent syllables, the first will be realized as a falling pitch rather than a high pitch. While in single words the rightmost stress is the strongest, an intonational contour exists over utterances which goes from high to low and ends with a boundary low pitch.
new_statements.citation: Tuttle, Siri G. 1990. Tolowa Prosody - an Interim Report. Typescript, University of Washington, 2 Dec 1990 (paper for the XXIXth Conference on American Indian Languages, AAA New Orleans), 6 pp; scan also carries the AAA abstract 'Stress, Accent, and Vowel Length in Tolowa'. Alaska Native Language Archive item CA990T1990.
new_statements.locator: Typescript p. 3 (PDF sheet 2, left half), sec. III 'Phonological and Phonetic Realization of Accent', A 'Proposed Rules for Accentuation' and B 'Phonetic Realization'; also p. 1 sec. I 'Tonal Status', p. 6 sec. VI 'Conclusion', and the AAA abstract on PDF sheet 5 (Abstracts p. 229). Quotes verified against the page scan.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: I extracted the sheets with pdfimages and read the page scan, not only the scanned. Typescript p. 3 (sheet 2, left half), sec. III.A-B: 'The domain of stress is bounded by the right edge of the stem. / Stress the last vowel in the domain. / Stress all full vowels. / The strongest stress in a word is the rightmost stress.. An accented vowel is realized with high pitch. Generally, if there are two accented vowels in adjacent syllables, the first will be realized as a falling pitch rather than a high pitch. While in single words the rightmost stress is the strongest, an intonational contour exists over utterances which goes from high to low and ends with a boundary low pitch.' -- word for word…
new_statements.relation_note: Chetco is not in the catalog; the one existing statement (Bright 1964, Smith River Tolowa: pitch accent or tone, morphologically determined) is compatible. Tuttle supplies the placement rules Bright lacked: the domain is bounded by the stem's right edge, the stem vowel takes the strongest stress, full vowels elsewhere take lesser stress, and accent is realized as high pitch with intonational deletion utterance-finally. She describes the same variety as Bright (Smith River Tolowa, consultants Samuel Lopez, Edward G. Richards Jr. and Berneice Humphrey of Smith River, California), not Chetco proper; her abstract's paraphrase of Bright as 'penultimate stress' differs in wording from Bright's ow…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The stress domain ends at the right edge of the stem; the last vowel of that domain (the stem vowel) is stressed, every full (non-schwa) vowel is also stressed, and the rightmost stress, i.e. the stem's, is the strongest in the word. Accent is realized as high pitch (falling pitch on the first of two adjacent accented vowels). Tuttle calls the system a 'pitch accent' (p. 6) and states on p. 1 that 'Tolowa is not classed as a tone language, like Navajo or Chipewyan'; her AAA abstract adds that 'stress appears as high pitch, triggering vowel lengthening; competing accentual high pitch deletes pitch stress, leaving a low-pitched long vowel'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rules 3-4 (p. 3) give a multi-stress system: all full vowels in prefixes and stems carry stress, with the rightmost (stem) stress the strongest; prefix schwas are unstressed, and suffix full vowels are not stressed (predictions IV.A-C, p. 3; examples p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 5 'Problems': the distinctions between long high, falling and low pitches on prefix syllables ('The Three [e]s') remain unresolved, and stem pitch may be lost after a full vowel in the prefixes; p. 6: 'I suggest that optionally, high pitch on a stem may be deleted when there is a preceding stressed vowel and the stem is utterance final' (in sentences 'final high pitches are routinely lost', while the same forms with a suffix keep the stem pitch). The conclusion notes 'tone-like phenomena (the opacity of prefixes like 2pl [u'] and variation between treatments of phonetically similar prefixes)'. The AAA abstract (p. 229) reports Tuttle's reading of Bright 1964 as 'penultimate stress, marked with high pitch' with exceptions, and that Seaburg's data show final high pitches.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuttle 1990 describes Tolowa (Smith River Athapaskan) from Seaburg's 1976-82 notes (Samuel Lopez, Edward G. Richards Jr.) and her own work with Berneice Humphrey of Smith River, California; it does not mention Chetco. chet1237 is a Glottolog bookkeeping code for the Chetco variety, which Glottolog groups with Tolowa under Tolowa-Chetco (tolo1259); Bright 1964:101 calls Smith River 'almost mutually intelligible' with the Chetco and Winchuck river dialects. No first-hand Chetco stress rule exists in the opened sources; Jacobs & Seaburg 1976 (held held by the project) only preserve Jacobs' 1935 stress marks on a Chetco text without a rule.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. Bright 1964 (existing statement) describes a pitch accent system with distributional constraints and no explicit placement rule; Tuttle 1990 makes the placement morphological (stem-bounded, stem vowel strongest, realized as high pitch) and keeps the 'pitch accent' label. One wording tension: Tuttle's AAA abstract summarizes Bright as 'penultimate stress, marked with high pitch' while her own rules put the strongest stress on the rightmost (stem) vowel, and she notes that Seaburg's data show final high pitches that Bright's account did not predict; the typescript treats those final highs as regular and their loss as intonational. Both sources describe Smith River Tolowa rather than Chetco proper, so any statement for chet1237 rests on the near-mutual-intelligibility Bright asserts (p. 101) between Smith River and the Chetco/Winchuck dialects.

sources.note: p.104 sec.3: 'pitch accent or tone, with at least two degrees of prominence'; high pitch limited by constraints a-d (monosyllables high; every utterance >=1 high; no all-high/all-low polysyllables; max two highs per word); summarised as 'a pitch accent system, in contrast with a pitch system like that of Navaho'.
